lessons.title: German rule in Kamerun (1884–1916)
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level History — Colonial rule in Cameroon (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Explain how Germany took control of Kamerun
Describe German administration and economic activity
Assess the effects of German rule on the people
reviewNotes: Historian to verify: the treaty date of 12 July 1884 (given only as July 1884), the Berlin Conference dates, the neutrality of the 'effects' lists, the size of Kamerun in 1914 (the 1911 enlargement is deliberately not mentioned) and the names of resistance leaders and events (not named on purpose).

Draft for historian review: only widely accepted facts and approximate dates are used; every date, name and interpretation must be verified by a history teacher before release. Political questions are stated neutrally.

blocks.md: In the 1880s European powers competed for territory in Africa, a period often called the **Scramble for Africa**. The **Berlin Conference** (1884–1885) set rules for dividing African territory among European powers. In **July 1884** German representatives signed treaties with Duala chiefs on the Wouri, and Germany declared the territory a protectorate called **Kamerun**.

blocks.caption: German Kamerun on a timeline
blocks.alt: A timeline with 1884, 1914, 1916 and 1922 and a bar for German rule between 1884 and 1916.

blocks.title: How Germany expanded
blocks.md: From the coast the Germans moved inland by treaties, military expeditions and the building of posts. Resistance came from many peoples; some were defeated after fighting, while others negotiated. Agreements with Britain and France later fixed the borders. By 1914 Kamerun covered a large area of Central Africa.

**Administration.** A governor and district officers ruled; German officials often governed through local chiefs but used force and taxes. Capital cities and military posts were set up. **Economy.** Germany developed plantations (cocoa, banana, rubber, palm oil) on land taken around Mount Cameroon, built roads, wharves and **railways** at Douala, and relied heavily on forced and low-paid labour.

blocks.title: Effects
blocks.md:
- Roads, ports, railways and plantations were built.
- Missions and some schools taught in German and local languages.
- Land was taken from local people and forced labour was widely used.
- Local rulers lost power; many people suffered violent conflict and heavy taxes.
- The borders that Germany fixed with Britain and France shaped later boundaries.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md: Describe German rule neutrally and factually: it brought infrastructure and also hardship and loss of independence. Avoid one-sided phrases. Exact details of the Duala treaty and of resistance leaders are matters on which historians write at length; give only what you are sure of.

blocks.title: Example 1: causes
blocks.statement: Give two reasons why European powers took over African territory in the late 1800s.
steps: They wanted raw materials and markets for their industries.
Competition between powers and national pride encouraged claiming land.
Better weapons and medicines made inland travel possible.
blocks.answer: Economic interests (raw materials, markets) and rivalry between powers.

blocks.title: Example 2: effects
blocks.statement: State one positive and one negative effect of German rule in Kamerun.
steps: Positive: railways, roads and ports were built.
Negative: land was taken and forced labour was widespread.
Both are well documented in the sources.
blocks.answer: Positive: infrastructure; negative: loss of land and forced labour.

lessons.title: The First World War in Cameroon, mandates and trusteeship
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level History — Colonial rule in Cameroon (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe how the First World War affected Kamerun
Explain the partition of Kamerun and the League of Nations mandates
Compare British and French administration in general terms
Explain the change from mandates to trusteeship
reviewNotes: Historian to verify: the campaign chronology (Douala 1914, German surrender in early 1916), the division of 1916 (France received the larger part) and the 1919/1922 legal steps (not detailed), mandate duties, British administration with Nigeria, and the Trusteeship date (1946).

Draft for historian review: only widely accepted facts and approximate dates are used; every date, name and interpretation must be verified by a history teacher before release. Political questions are stated neutrally.

blocks.md: In **1914** the First World War began in Europe and spread to Africa. British, French and Belgian forces attacked German Kamerun from several directions. The coast and **Douala** fell to the Allies in 1914. German forces retreated inland and held out in some places until early **1916**, when the last German forces left for Spanish territory and the war in Kamerun ended.

blocks.caption: From the First World War to the Trusteeship

blocks.title: Partition
blocks.md: After the German defeat, Britain and France administered Kamerun together for a time and then divided it in 1916: France received the larger eastern part and Britain two narrow strips along the Nigerian border. The **League of Nations** (founded after the war) confirmed these arrangements as **mandates** in **1922**: **British Cameroons** and **French Cameroun**.

A **mandate** was a territory taken from a defeated country and entrusted to another power to administer, with the duty to prepare the people for self-government and to report to the League. The **British Cameroons** was divided into **Northern** and **Southern Cameroons** and administered as part of neighbouring **Nigeria**. **French Cameroun** was administered separately.

blocks.title: Styles of rule
blocks.md: Britain generally used **indirect rule**, working through local chiefs and councils under British supervision. France used more **direct administration**, with French officials and a policy of cultural assimilation as a goal. Both used taxes and forced labour in the early years, and both built roads, schools and clinics at different speeds.

blocks.title: From mandate to trusteeship
blocks.md: After the Second World War the League was replaced by the **United Nations** (1945). Mandates became **Trust Territories** under UN supervision in **1946**: the British Cameroons and French Cameroun were placed under the UN **Trusteeship** system. Trust powers had to prepare the people for self-government or independence and report to the UN.

blocks.title: Example 1: define the mandate
blocks.statement: Explain the difference between a colony and a mandate.
steps: A colony is ruled by a foreign power for its own interests.
A mandate was held in trust under the League of Nations, with duties to the people and reports to the League.
The mandate power did not own the territory.
blocks.answer: A mandate was a trust held under the League's supervision, not outright ownership.

blocks.title: Example 2: sequence
blocks.statement: Put in order: UN Trusteeship, League of Nations mandates, end of German rule.
blocks.answer: End of German rule, mandates, Trusteeship.
